subject: evasive movement combined with blind strip under plane

messages.subject: evasive movement combined with blind strip under plane
parts:
Hi all (2)

=20

After such a speedy response to my first question today I am now
encouraged to ask another!

=20

Our aerial survey data of seaducks show evidence of evasive movement in
response to the plane (and the surveyors describe this too). This is
combined with a limitation in the data collection, since the observers
cannot see the sea surface beneath the plane to a distance of 44m either
side. The data are collected as cluster sizes in 4 bands which get wider
with distance from the plane.

=20

The problem is that an unknown proportion of the birds underneath the
plane are moving away from the flight path into the visible area,
leaving an equally unknown proportion behind. In addition there appears
to be evasive movement in the visible area too, with band B being higher
than band A.

I've looked through the archives for ways to tackle this kind of
problem, and none of the entries quite seem to match this problem.

=20

So far my approach has been to reduce the observation distances and
cut-points by 44m prior to analysis and assume that detection at 44m is
1 (although this obviously ignores the higher peak in B). To account for
the rising numbers between A and B I have fitted a haz-rate function
which splits the difference. However, I am concerned that I am risking
over-estimation of D, since the plane may have effectively squeezed all
the birds present near the transect (but un-observable) into a smaller
(but observable) area (i.e. the strip beneath the plane is 'empty' and
the surveyed area next to the plane has elevated numbers).

=20

I have been trying to come up with solutions to this based on the area
surveyed etc but have no solid answers yet.

=20

One I idea I had was if I could manually add 44m to the estimate of ESW
and then re-calculate D - would this only be valid under the assumption
that all birds have moved out of the 'blind' strip? (if so then this may
be a moderately acceptable assumption to make). If this is ok then I am
not sure how to re-calculate the variance estimators...=20

=20

Any help gratefully received.

=20

Mark
